food.text: The Kingdom of Zimbabwe (c. 1220 to 1450) was a Shona kingdom whose economy rested on cattle herding, farming and gold mining. Its capital at Great Zimbabwe was the largest stone structure in precolonial Southern Africa.

The Kingdom of Kongo appeared in the thirteenth century and was divided into six provinces. Trade was its main activity, and that trade was based on highly productive agriculture and increasing exploitation of mineral wealth.

The Kingdom of Mapungubwe (c. 1075 to c. 1220) lay between the Shashe and Limpopo Rivers. Its society was mainly centered around family and farming, and at its height the capital's population was about 5000 people.

Millet was the main staple in the region that maize and cassava would later replace. Those crops came through trade with the Portuguese at their ports at Luanda and Benguela, and they caused population growth in the region and other parts of Africa.

art.text: Great Zimbabwe is the largest stone structure in precolonial Southern Africa, and its stone city spans 7.22 square kilometres. Major construction lasted from the 11th century to the 15th, and the city was abandoned in the 16th or 17th century.

Great Zimbabwe is the largest stone structure in precolonial Southern Africa. Major construction began in the 11th century and continued until the 15th century. The stone city spans an area of 7.22 square kilometres.

The Zimbabwe Bird is a soapstone sculpture from the ruins of the medieval city of Great Zimbabwe. The birds stand about 40 centimetres tall on columns more than 90 cm tall, and were originally installed on walls and monoliths. Nothing like them has been discovered elsewhere.

Zimbabwe is distinctive in Africa for its large number of medieval city ruins built in a unique dry stone style. The most famous are the Great Zimbabwe ruins in Masvingo. Other ruins include Khami, Dhlo-Dhlo, and Naletale.

The symbolism of the Zimbabwe birds is debated. They more probably represent sacred or totemic animals of the Shona, such as the bateleur eagle (chapungu), held to be a messenger from Mwari and the ancestors, or the fish eagle (hungwe), possibly the original Shona totem.

Fifteenth-century Kongo Christian religious art objects were closely modeled on European prototypes. They were usually cast in an open mold using metal obtained from brass units of currency called manillas, imported from Europe.

The ruling dynasty of Great Zimbabwe used its wealth to build houses out of thick daga, an earthen daub, rather than daga and poles. They also built stone walls to shield themselves from public view. This process advanced rapidly in the 13th century and produced large dry-stone walls.
At the centre of Great Zimbabwe stood the Great Enclosure, which is thought to have housed royalty and had demarcated spaces for rituals. Commoners lived around it, within the second perimeter wall.

Afonso, who ruled Nsundi province and later became king of Kongo, embraced Christianity after the Portuguese arrived in 1491. Around the time his father turned against the priests, Afonso ordered the destruction of traditional art objects that might offend Portuguese sensibilities. Many in the realm were displeased.

The Portuguese who first reached M'banza-Kongo in 1491 travelled ten days from the mouth of the Congo River. Its Cathedral of the Holy Saviour of Congo, built in 1491, has ruins that many Angolans claim belong to the oldest church in sub-Saharan Africa.

art.text: James Theodore Bent investigated the Great Zimbabwe ruins in 1891 and recorded eight birds, six large and two small. He thought there had probably been more, since several additional stone pedestals had their tops broken off.

war.text: In the 15th century, the Kingdom of Kongo pushed its conquests eastward. There it ran into the Tio Kingdom, which halted Kongo's expansion. The Tio state, founded around the 14th century, rivalled Kongo for much of its early existence.

Around 1490, a civil conflict shook the Mutapa Empire. According to Diogo de Alcáçova's 1506 report, rumours that Changamire was plotting for the kingship led Mukombero to order him to undergo a poison trial, in which drinking the poison (muteyo) and being harmed by it meant guilt. Instead, Changamire led an army to Mukombwe's zimbabwe, killed him, and took the kingship. He is also said to have killed 21 of Mukombero's sons, with Chikuyo Chisamarengu the only one to escape.

After the death of Nzinga a Nkuwu in 1506, his son Afonso prevailed in a brief civil war against his brother and became the sixth king of Kongo. The strongest opposition came from his half brother Mpanzu a Kitima, who rebelled, raised an army in the provinces and planned to march on the capital, Mbanza Kongo. Mpanzu a Kitima was killed in the fighting, either by falling into a punji trap during his army's rout or by being captured and then executed.

In 1491 the manikongo, the king of Kongo, asked the Portuguese for help against the Tio. Kongo's eastward conquests had already been halted by the Tio Kingdom in the 15th century. The request shows how war helped draw Portugal into Central Africa.

From the 12th century, Great Zimbabwe wrestled with other settlements, such as Chivowa, for economic and political dominance in the Southern Zambezi Escarpment. Its rise was rapid, and by 1250 it had become an important trade centre.

Around 1494, Chikuyo returned with a large army and fought Changamire I in a deadly battle that lasted over 3 days and ended with Changamire I's death. Chikuyo then took the kingship and consolidated his rule over the empire, except for Guruuswa, which stayed loyal to Changamire II. Over the following decades the Munhumutapa is known to have fought Changamire II intermittently, until at least 1512.

The Mutapa Empire's founder Mutota is said to have been a hunter-warrior in the militaristic Nzou Samanyanga clan. He led the clan to conquer Dande. He then extended his rule over Guruuswa, a territory to the south, before his death.

According to Shona tradition, Mutota's son Matope expanded the young Mutapa state through numerous military campaigns, first conquering all Tavara and Tonga from the Musengezi River eastwards to the Ruenya River. The Tavara, led by the Nhari Unendoro clan, fiercely resisted him, and he subdued them only when Karuva's son Chikuma betrayed the Tavara, by giving away their armies' positions or by siding with Matope. Matope also established several vassals, including Barue, Uteve and Manyika.

Afonso I did more than defend his throne. As king he centralized power at Mbanza Kongo and curtailed the power of the nobility. He expanded the kingdom's borders through war, launching campaigns to the south and east. Captives taken in those wars were enslaved and forcibly relocated to Mbanza Kongo, while conquered lands paid tribute in iron, palm cloth and ivory.

Around 1000 to 1500, the gold of the interior was a prize that states in Southern Africa competed over. Suleiman Hassan of Kilwa, who ruled c. 1178 to 1195, wrested control of the city of Sofala from the Mogadishans. Sofala was the main entrepot for the gold and ivory trade with Great Zimbabwe, and its gold revenues financed Kilwa's expansion.

Around 1494, Chikuyo returned with a large army and fought a long and deadly battle against Changamire I, who had killed his father, the king, and is said to have killed 21 of the king's sons. Changamire I died in the battle, and Chikuyo took the kingship. Not every part of the Mutapa Empire accepted his victory: Guruuswa stayed loyal to Changamire II, the successor of the dead rival. Over the following decades the Mwenemutapa fought Changamire II intermittently, until at least 1512, with Changamire II likely aided by Butua.

In the Battle of Mbanza Kongo, the chronicler Paiva Manso said Mpanzu a Kitima's army fled in terror, though it outnumbered Afonso's. The cause, he wrote, was the sight of Saint James the Great and five heavenly armored horsemen in the sky. The story may be an allegory for a coup against anti-Catholic elements in the royal house.

In the Luba oral tradition, Nkongolo was red-skinned and notorious for his cruelty, using a curved nkololo knife to mutilate people. When his mother laughed at him after he lost games to Kalala Ilunga, he had her buried alive. Ilunga saw black ants carrying off termites, took it as a sign to make war, and killed some of Nkongolo's men. With the help of a drummer he discovered a trap meant to kill him and fled east across the Congo. He later returned with an army, captured Nkongolo and executed him, burying his head and genitals in a sacred basket.

Luba tradition says Kasongo Mwine Kibanza had four physically abnormal children, who were barred from succession. His son Ilunga Mpunji was caught with Kasongo's senior wife, and the two were drowned; another son died of grief. When their spirits terrorised the people, Kasongo consulted the diviner of the spirit Nkulu and killed them. After Kasongo Mwine Kibanza died, the other claimants to succeed him died, one from a snake bite and one from a leopard. Kasongo Bisonwe, now Kasongo Kabundulu, defeated another claimant in battle to become ruler.

literature.text: King Nzinga a Nkuwu of Kongo sent a large mission headed by the noble Kala ka Mfusu to Europe. The envoys stayed for nearly four years, studying Christianity and learning reading and writing. The mission returned to Kongo in 1491, when the king was baptised as João I.

The origins of the Mbundu people are kept in oral traditions passed down through the generations. One tradition says the Mbundu came from "the great water", which many historians interpret as the Atlantic Ocean. It also names five great ancestors, among them Kajinga ka Mbulu, founder of the Mbondo Kingdom.

Detailed written descriptions of the Kongo people, their language and their infrastructure at the Atlantic ports appear in the 15th century, composed by Portuguese explorers. According to Vansina, any documented history of the Kongo from before this period has not survived into the modern era.

Kongo's royal embassy reached Lisbon in late 1486 and stayed nearly four years with the monks of Saint John the Baptist. There they studied Christianity and Portuguese with Vicente dos Anjos, who also learned to speak Kikongo. This exchange began a Kongolese version of Christianity.

A second Mbundu oral tradition says a man named Mussuri rose from ironworker to king of the Mbundu. He married a woman named Ngola Inene, and their daughter Samba gave birth to 8 children. Those children later begot the Ndongo, Mbondo, Pende, Hungu, Lenge, Imbangala, Songo and Libolo peoples.

The Pende tell of a single ancestor, Ngola Kilanji, who led his people from Tandji near the Zambezi River west to Luanda on the coast. There he joined a group led by the master blacksmith Bembo Kalamba, whose people taught farming, cattle-herding and weaving. The royal title ngola is said to come from his name.

Diogo Cão raised stone pillars called padrões along the African coast. Inscriptions on two of them, at Cape Santa Maria and Cape Cross, are dated 1482 and 1485 and can still be read. The Cape Cross pillar was long in Berlin before being returned to Namibia.

science.text: Construction of the stone buildings at Great Zimbabwe started in the 11th century and continued until the 15th century. The Great Enclosure, with its large dry-stone walls, was built during the 13th and 14th centuries. The city is the largest stone structure in precolonial Southern Africa.

By the 15th century the Bakongo were unified as the Kingdom of Kongo under a ruler called the manikongo. They were experts in metalwork, pottery, and weaving raffia cloth. They also stimulated interregional trade through a tribute system controlled by the manikongo.

Portuguese caravels commanded by Diogo Cão arrived in the Congo in 1482, and close relations with the Kingdom of Kongo were soon established. The Portuguese brought firearms and many other technological advances, as well as a new religion, Christianity. In return, the King of the Congo offered plenty of slaves, along with ivory and minerals, so that human beings were part of what Kongo traded for Portuguese weapons and technology.

In August 1482, Diogo Cão arrived at the mouth of the Congo River and marked it with a padrão erected on Shark Point, commemorating the Portuguese occupation. The marker stood until 1642, when the Dutch destroyed it during their occupation of the Congo.

On his second voyage of 1484–1486, Diogo Cão revisited the Congo and erected two more padrões beyond his previous voyage, at Cabo Negro, Angola, and at Cape Cross. The Cape Cross pillar probably marked the end of his progress southward, some 1,400 kilometers.
Dhaka pits at Great Zimbabwe were closed depressions used for water management as reservoirs, wells and springs. The system could hold more than 18,000 cubic metres of water.

All four pillars set up by Diogo Cão on his two voyages have been found still on their original sites. Inscriptions on the Cape Santa Maria and Cape Cross pillars, dated 1482 and 1485, can still be read. The Cape Cross padrão was long in Berlin before being returned to Namibia.

politics.text: By the 15th century the farming Bakongo people were unified as the Kingdom of Kongo under a ruler called the manikongo. He lived in the fertile Pool Malebo area on the lower Congo River, and the capital was M'banza-Kongo.

The Kingdom of Kongo was founded around 1390 through a political marriage between two Kikongo-speaking peoples. Nima a Nzima, ruler of the Mpemba Kasi and Vungu, wed Lukeni lua Nsanze, daughter of Nsaku lau, ruler of the neighbouring Mbata Kingdom.

Great Zimbabwe was the capital of a Shona kingdom and the largest stone structure in precolonial Southern Africa. Around 1300 it replaced Mapungubwe as the most important trading centre in the interior, exporting gold via Swahili city-states into the Indian Ocean trade.

Oral tradition says Nyatsimba Mutota led part of Great Zimbabwe's population north in search of salt and founded the Mutapa Empire. He took the title mwene mutupa, meaning Lord of the Conquered Land, and became the high priest of Mwari.

In the Limpopo-Shashe Basin, states and chiefdoms competed over gold and other goods for the Indian Ocean trade from the 10th century. By 1300, trade routes had shifted north as merchants bypassed Mapungubwe to reach the gold-producing interior. This precipitated Mapungubwe's rapid decline and the dominance of Great Zimbabwe.

Portuguese explorers reached the Kingdom of Kongo in 1483 and found a centralized government, a currency called nzimbu, and markets. The king Nzinga a Nkuwu was baptized in 1491 and took the name João I.

The Bakongo stimulated interregional trade through a tribute system controlled by the manikongo. With superior organization they conquered their neighbors and extracted tribute, and they were also experts in metalwork, pottery and weaving raffia cloth.

The Mbata Kingdom held a privileged position, being a kingdom within the Kingdom of Kongo. Its king was not appointed by the Manikongo but inherited through the matrilineal line from Lukeni Luansanze's descendants. Its princes were traditionally responsible for Kongo's diplomacy.

The Zimbabwe state was made up of over 150 smaller zimbabwes and likely covered 50,000 square kilometres. Its ruling dynasty used its wealth to build stone walls to shield themselves from public view, and the Great Enclosure is thought to have housed royalty.

Mbata's powerful army was essential in the conquest of the kingdom of Mwene Kabunga, on a mountainous plateau to the south. This consolidated the territory behind the Kingdom of Kongo, and Lukemi Lua Nimi took the title Mwene Kongo, meaning king of all the kingdoms of Kongo.

Nyatsimba Mutota lost a war with his kinsman Mukwati and fled Great Zimbabwe, which was already losing power to a rival capital at Ingombe Ilede near the Zambezi. Around 1440 he began aggressive campaigns against the surrounding tribes, expanding his lands to the west along the Zambezi. He introduced the tradition of appointing his sons as vassals over the conquered lands.
Mutota conquered Great Zimbabwe before his death, and it remained a cult center. He died around 1450 after a war with a Tonga/Korekore tribe and was succeeded by his son Matope Nyanhehwe Nebedza.

Elites at Great Zimbabwe possibly expanded regional trading networks as international gold demand fell in the early 15th century. By the late 15th century, offshoots of the royal family formed new dynasties, possibly after losing succession disputes. Angoche traders then opened a Zambezi route that helped Khami, capital of the Kingdom of Butua, rise.

philosophy.text: Traditional Kongo religion names a Creator God, Nzambi Ampungu, who gave birth to the universe and the spirits who live in it. Yet ancestor veneration, not the creator, is described as the core principle of the spirituality.

The Kongo people were among the earliest indigenous Africans to welcome Portuguese traders in 1483. The Portuguese found them open to ideas, and they began converting to Catholicism in the late 15th century.

The Bakongo divide the cosmos into two worlds: the top half is the physical world, ku nseke, and the bottom half is the spiritual world, ku mpèmba. Expert healers called Banganga train extensively so they can commune with the ancestors in the spiritual realms and seek their guidance.

Nzinga-a-Nkuwu could not politically afford to give up polygamy. Power in Kongo was elective rather than hereditary, and the culture was matrilineal, so the king's elder son was not automatically the next king.

Researcher Molefi Kete Asante describes four moments of the sun in Bakongo thought: rising, peaking, setting and absence. They match the four stages of life, which are conception, birth, maturity and death. Everything, even ideas, passes through them, and the cycle is drawn as a circle with a cross inside, the Yowa or dikenga cosmogram.

Because the Kingdom of Kongo was so centralized, its leaders could influence traditional religious practice across the Congo Basin. Other groups in West-Central Africa, such as the Chokwe and Ambundu, adopted elements of Bakongo spirituality.
When Diogo Cão sailed back to Portugal, he carried a party of Kongo emissaries. In Lisbon they were baptised and placed in a monastery before returning to the king in 1491.
At the 1491 baptism, only the king and his nobles were meant to convert, but the queen demanded to be baptised too. The royal family took Portuguese names: João, Leonor and Afonso.

Historians John K. Thornton and Linda M. Heywood note that Central Africans probably never agreed on the details of their cosmology, a product of what they call continuous revelation and precarious priesthood. Thornton adds that written descriptions from missionary and colonial records carry a hostile bias.

culture.text: When the Portuguese reached the Kongo people in 1483, they found a kingdom with a centralized government, a currency called nzimbu, and markets. They also found well developed transport infrastructure inland from the Atlantic port settlement.

King Nzinga a Nkuwu of Kongo was baptised on 3 May 1491 and took the Portuguese name João. He abandoned the new faith in 1495, partly because the Church required monogamy. In Kongo, power was elective rather than hereditary, so he could not give up polygamy.

Kongo's royal family took Portuguese names in 1491, including João, Leonor and Afonso. Initially only the king and his nobles were to be converted, but the queen demanded to be baptised. A thousand subjects were detailed to help the Portuguese carpenters build a church. Meanwhile Portuguese soldiers accompanied the king on a campaign to defend the province of Nsundi from Bateke raiders, where European firearms were decisive in the victory and many captives were taken.

Under Afonso I, the Kongolese aristocracy adopted Portuguese names, titles, coats of arms and styles of dress. Youths from elite families were sent to Europe for education, and Christian festivals were observed. To the displeasure of many, he also ordered the destruction of traditional art objects that might offend Portuguese sensibilities.

In the middle ages, Muslims of the Swahili coast traded with Great Zimbabwe. They brought luxuries across the Indian Ocean from outposts such as Sofala in exchange for gold. The economy of the Kilwa Sultanate depended on this gold trade.
At the heart of Great Zimbabwe stood the Great Enclosure, thought to have housed royalty. It had demarcated spaces for rituals, while commoners lived around it inside the second perimeter wall.

The Tio Kingdom's king was thought to derive authority from mystical prowess. Evidence is a series of six anvils dedicated to the king and five lords, located near the Falls of Lefini, where Nkwe Mbali, the national nature spirit, was believed to reside.

In 1491 Diogo Cão returned to Kongo accompanied by Catholic priests and soldiers. They baptised King Nzinga a Nkuwu, who took the name João I in honour of Portugal's king, João II. The king's principal nobles, starting with the ruler of Soyo, were baptised as well.
The association of kingship with smithing is believed to have originated among the Tio. It then spread to the kingdoms of Loango and Kongo.

Around 1390, the Kingdom of Kongo was founded through a political marriage between Nima a Nzima and Lukeni lua Nsanze. Lukeni lua Nimi's ally, the Mwene Kabunga, held lands with a shrine. Two centuries later, the Mwene Kabunga's descendants still symbolically challenged the conquest in an annual celebration.

As Lukeni lua Nimi expanded the young Kingdom of Kongo, he allied with the Mwene Kabunga, whose lands held a shrine. Two centuries later, the Mwene Kabunga's descendants still symbolically challenged the conquest in an annual celebration.
